title: A Jesuit pope
hookLine: Francis brought discernment into the language of the whole Church

lines: THE WORD GOES TO THE KITCHENS.
cards: Discernment can sound like a word for retreat houses and novitiates: quiet rooms, a spiritual director, someone deciding whether to become a priest or a sister.
Then a Jesuit from Buenos Aires, Jorge Mario Bergoglio, became Pope Francis, whom you met on day nine hundred thirty-three. The word came with him.
It turned up in his letters to the whole Church, in his talks to young people, in what he said to married couples, in the way he asked bishops to meet and listen.
A retreat-house word went out into kitchens and parish halls.

teach.h: A POPE FORMED BY THE EXERCISES.
teach.b: A Jesuit pope. Francis had made the Spiritual Exercises, had given them to others, and had been a novice master and a Jesuit provincial in Argentina. So when he wrote, the Ignatian vocabulary came along.
In his letter on holiness, Rejoice and Be Glad, he gives the closing pages of a chapter to discernment.
It isn't only for rare, dramatic decisions, he says, but for daily life: small choices, ordinary days.
He recommends something familiar from this path: a sincere daily examination of conscience, looking back over the day with God.

teach.h: A GIFT TO ASK FOR, AND LISTENING.
teach.b: And he insists it's a gift to ask for, not a technique to master, and that it means listening: to God, to others, to reality, and especially to the poor.

Saint Paul gives the old instruction in the Douay-Rheims: "But prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Prove means test, try out. Francis asked every Catholic to do that, not only people in retreat houses.
He also brought the word into how the Church makes decisions, asking for meetings where people would pray, speak freely, listen, and then discern together, rather than simply vote.
Why it matters day to day: discernment isn't the same as deciding. Deciding asks what do I want.

teach.h: PROVE ALL THINGS; HOLD FAST THAT WHICH IS GOOD.
teach.b: Discernment asks, in the quiet, which of these good options draws me toward God and others, and which pulls me inward and away? It's the whole Jesuit vocabulary of these weeks, handed to everyone.

how: Following Pope Francis, Catholic parishes, families and Church gatherings speak of discernment as prayerful listening to God and one another before making choices, often alongside the daily examen.

o: a pope formed by the Exercises who spread discernment
the head of the Jesuits, nicknamed the black pope
a pope who made all priests take a Jesuit retreat

games.q: a Jesuit pope — tap the pairs.
p: which way draws me toward love?

s: Francis said discernment is only for big life decisions
he said it's for daily life too, and recommended a daily examen.
Francis described discernment as a gift to ask for, not just a technique
and as listening to God, to others and to reality.
discernment is the same as deciding what you want
it asks which good option draws you toward God and others.

games.q: you're a bishop at a Church meeting called by Francis. a hard question is on the table. what does he ask you to do?
o: pray, speak freely, listen, and discern together.
games.why: he asked for meetings shaped by prayer and listening, carrying the Jesuit word discernment into how the Church decides.

practice: Bring to mind a real, small decision in front of you, and hold the first option for a few breaths, noticing what moves in you: peace, restlessness, energy, dread.
Then hold the second the same way, and without deciding yet, notice which draws you outward, toward God and others, and which pulls you inward. If you pray, ask for light.

wordCard.voice: A Jesuit pope. Pope Francis, formed by the Spiritual Exercises, who carried the language of discernment from retreat houses into the life of the whole Church. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: discern. Not only what do I want, but which way draws toward love. See you tomorrow.
